proof:
# A nonnegative convex-body marginal dominates an explicit uniform law

Let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d, d>=1, and let
Y be a nonconstant affine functional of its uniform point, normalized
so that min_K Y=0. Write b=max_K Y>0, mu=E Y>0, and F(t)=P(Y<=t).
Then

    mu F(t) <= d t/(d+1) for every t>=0.          (1)

Equivalently, Y stochastically dominates the uniform distribution on
[0,(d+1)mu/d]:

    P(Y>=t) >= [1-d t/((d+1)mu)]_+ for t>=0.     (2)

The coefficient in(1), or the interval length in(2), is sharp. This is
a one-dimensional marginal inequality, not a proof of OC.

## 1. Two Brunn--Minkowski bounds at a prescribed cut

The marginal is nonatomic, its support is[0,b], and F(0)=0,F(b)=1.
Ordinary Brunn--Minkowski applied to lower and upper cap bodies shows
that F^(1/d) and(1-F)^(1/d) are concave on[0,b]. For example, the
Minkowski average of the two lower cap bodies at s and t is contained
in the lower cap at the averaged threshold. The same inclusion holds
for upper caps. All volumes here are normalized by|K|.

Fix0<t<b and put alpha=F(t) in(0,1), q=(1-alpha)^(1/d) in(0,1).
Lower-cap root concavity gives

    F(s)>=alpha(s/t)^d,             0<=s<=t.      (3)

Upper-cap root concavity says that every secant slope after t is at
most the secant slope from0 to t. Thus

    1-F(s)<=[1-(1-q)s/t]^d,         t<=s<=b.      (4)

The bracket is nonnegative on this entire interval: the same concavity
at b, or a limit from interior points with positive tail, implies
b<=t/(1-q). Beyond b the tail is zero. Consequently the bound by the
positive part of the affine power in(4) holds for all s>=t. This does
not extend a concave root by zero and claim the extension is concave.

Integrating the tail and using(3)-(4) gives

    mu/t <= 1-alpha/(d+1)+q^(d+1)/((d+1)(1-q))
          =[d+q^d/(1-q)]/(d+1).                  (5)

The second equality uses alpha=1-q^d.

## 2. Exact constant and endpoint cases

Multiply(5) by alpha. Since

    alpha/(1-q)=1+q+...+q^(d-1)<=d,

one has

    alpha[d+q^d/(1-q)]
       =d(1-q^d)+q^d(1+q+...+q^(d-1))<=d.

This proves(1) for0<t<b. At t=0 it is immediate. At t=b, the
lower-cap bound F(s)>=(s/b)^d gives

    mu=integral_0^b(1-F(s))ds<=db/(d+1).

For t>=b, F(t)=1 and this proves(1). Nonatomicity turns the CDF
inequality into the closed-tail statement(2), including at the two
support endpoints. For d>=2 the finite-cut product inequality is
strict when0<t<b; sharpness can still occur at b or as t decreases
to zero. No undefined power is used in d=1.

Take a convex cone whose cross-sections at height s in[0,b] have
(d-1)-volume proportional to s^(d-1). Then F(s)=(s/b)^d and
mu=db/(d+1), so equality holds in(1) at t=b. Also no longer uniform
interval can be stochastically dominated, because its upper tail at
b would be positive while the cone's upper tail there is zero.
For d=1 the original marginal is a uniform interval and equality in
(1) holds at every threshold in its support.

## 3. Positive simplex normals and the limitation of the comparison

For X uniform on r T_d, where T_d is the standard simplex, and any
w_i>=0 with sum_i w_i=1, the scalar Y=w dot X has minimum zero and
mean r/(d+1). Therefore

    |rT_d intersect{w dot X>=t}|
       >=|T_d| r^d [1-d t/r]_+.                  (6)

This applies with one common w and different affine thresholds on
different integer fibers. It compares those positive-normal caps to
a uniform interval[0,r/d] with total weight|T_d|r^d, or constant
one-dimensional density d|T_d|r^(d-1). It is a lower bound for
individual original cap masses, not an equality of source measures.

At the actual simplex centroid threshold t=r/(d+1), the right side
is only|T_d|r^d/(d+1). In d>=2 this is below the ordinary sharp
centroid payment Gamma_d|T_d|r^d. Thus this uniform comparison alone
cannot retain the exact OC constant; two exposed equal simplex fibers
already display that loss. Any use toward OC must retain additional
actual cap mass by a separately proved argument.
